The Standard in Brief

Default-Deny, stated in advance and enforced in code

Autonomous AI agents can already read data, draft transactions, and call tools. What they cannot safely do is hold open-ended authority over value on an immutable ledger: a language model produces probabilities, not guarantees, and once a transaction is mined, no apology or system prompt can reverse it. Instructions and data share the same channel in an AI model, so the constraint cannot live in the prompt — it must live in code that reverts when the rule is broken.

The Clearing House operates under an uncompromising Default-Deny execution policy. Contracts registered through the standard carry a hardcoded zero percent base fee, single-action boundary locks, and isolated state scopes to prevent exploit propagation. The agent never receives a key with general authority: the owner signs a permit that names one action in full, and the contract enforces that permit exactly as written, or reverts.

Anatomy of a permit: eight mandatory fields

If any field is absent, mismatched, expired, or already consumed, the permit does not partially execute — it fails in full.

#FieldWhat it binds
1Owner / SignerCryptographic authority granting the delegation.
2Agent (Grantee)The specific execution agent address allowed to invoke the action.
3Target ContractThe explicit smart contract allowed to be called.
4Action SelectorKeccak-256 selector restricting callable methods.
5Value LimitHard ceiling on token or ETH transfer per call.
6NonceSingle-use counter preventing replay attacks.
7DeadlineEpoch timestamp bound enforcing automatic expiry.
8Domain Separator (EIP-712)Binds execution strictly to one Chain ID and contract address.

The Default-Deny audit matrix

The exhaustive classification every contract is checked against. Category 1 vectors are denied outright; Category 2 guards are required in sequence; anything unlisted defaults to denied until a lead auditor clears it.

Category 1 — Denied

Strictly Prohibited (Unacceptable) Vectors

  1. delegatecall Exclusions. Arbitrary delegatecall execution allows untrusted code injection into state storage context. Strictly denied unless bound to immutable proxies.
  2. selfdestruct Opcodes. Opcode selfdestruct introduces unexpected state erasure and contract deletion vulnerabilities. Prohibited across all permits.
  3. Centralized onlyOwner Admin Keys. Unrestricted single-key owner privileges create rug-pull vectors. Admin actions must pass multi-sig or timelock permits.
  4. tx.origin Authentication. Using tx.origin for authorization exposes contracts to phishing reentrancy attacks. Must use msg.sender or signed permits.
  5. Inline Assembly (assembly { }). Unchecked low-level Yul assembly bypasses Solidity compiler safety checks. Prohibited except in audited cryptographic libs.
  6. Dynamic create / create2 Instantiation. Unbounded dynamic contract creation allows rogue deployments without pre-registration. DENIED by default.
  7. Block Timestamp / Number Reliance. Miner-manipulable timestamp logic for randomness or precise locks is denied; must use cryptographic chain Oracles.
  8. Unchecked Low-Level Calls. Raw target.call{value: val}("") without explicit boolean return checks and state mutation locks is strictly forbidden.
  9. Uninitialized Storage Pointers. Dangling storage struct pointers overwrite contract state variables unexpectedly. Compiler enforcement mandatory.

Category 2 — Required Guards

Adaptive (50/50 Trusted) Sequence Guards

  1. Reentrancy Lock Standard. Enforces nonReentrant status guards across state-changing functions to prevent recursive call hijacking.
  2. Check-Effects-Interactions Pattern. Requires state updates to execute before external asset transfers occur, mitigating reentrancy vulnerabilities.
  3. Immutable Constants Configuration. Critical addresses, clearing house roots, and protocol parameters must be assigned immutably at deployment.
  4. Single-Action Execution Boundaries. Restricts key transaction calls to single nonces or single-block boundaries to neutralize front-running bots.
  5. Lead-Auditor Catch-All Manual Review. Any unlisted or edge-case execution vector defaults to DENIED until reviewed and cleared by lead clearing auditors.

ILUSDTokenProtocol.sol Arbitrum Deployment

Sovereign Stable-Asset Engine & Creator Admin Minting

FEE: 0.00% BASE

Represents the historical ILUSD token protocol on Arbitrum Mainnet/One (Chain ID: 42161). Enforces sovereign stable-asset backing with zero-admin post-mint rules and strict creator privileges under Default-Deny clearing rules.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title ILUSDTokenProtocol - Creator Deployment on Arbitrum
/// @notice Sovereign asset permit engine under Default-Deny clearing rules
contract ILUSDTokenProtocol {
    string public constant name = "Interlocked USD";
    string public constant symbol = "ILUSD";
    uint8 public constant decimals = 18;
    uint256 public totalSupply;

    address public immutable creatorAdmin;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf;
    mapping(address => mapping(address => uint256)) public allowance;

    event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);
    event Approval(address indexed owner, address indexed spender, uint256 value);
    event CreatorMint(address indexed recipient, uint256 amount);

    constructor() {
        creatorAdmin = msg.sender;
    }

    modifier onlyCreatorAdmin() {
        require(msg.sender == creatorAdmin, "ILUSD: UNAUTHORIZED_CREATOR");
        _;
    }

    function mint(address recipient, uint256 amount) external onlyCreatorAdmin {
        totalSupply += amount;
        balanceOf[recipient] += amount;
        emit CreatorMint(recipient, amount);
        emit Transfer(address(0), recipient, amount);
    }

    function transfer(address recipient, uint256 amount) external returns (bool) {
        require(balanceOf[msg.sender] >= amount, "ILUSD: INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE");
        balanceOf[msg.sender] -= amount;
        balanceOf[recipient] += amount;
        emit Transfer(msg.sender, recipient, amount);
        return true;
    }

    function approve(address spender, uint256 amount) external returns (bool) {
        allowance[msg.sender][spender] = amount;
        emit Approval(msg.sender, spender, amount);
        return true;
    }
}

DBPreceptMessagingPermit.sol

Decoupled Sub-100 Line EVM Payload Delivery Contract

FEE: 0.00% BASE

On-chain message dispatch bound to a single-use permit hash: each (sender, payload, nonce) combination can execute exactly once.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title DBPreceptMessagingPermit - Decoupled On-Chain Message Dispatch
contract DBPreceptMessagingPermit {
    address public immutable clearingHouseAdmin;
    mapping(bytes32 => bool) public executedPermits;

    event MessageDispatched(bytes32 indexed permitHash, address indexed sender, string payload);

    constructor() {
        clearingHouseAdmin = msg.sender;
    }

    function dispatchVerifiedMessage(string memory payload, uint256 nonce) external {
        bytes32 permitHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, payload, nonce));
        require(!executedPermits[permitHash], "DBP: PERMIT_ALREADY_USED");
        executedPermits[permitHash] = true;
        emit MessageDispatched(permitHash, msg.sender, payload);
    }
}
03

DBPreceptVaultTransferPermit.sol

Zero-Fee Isolated Asset Transfer Guard with Reentrancy Locks

FEE: 0.00% BASE

Non-reentrant asset routing: only the vault owner can execute, every transfer hash is single-use, and state updates precede the external call.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title DBPreceptVaultTransferPermit - Non-Reentrant Asset Routing
contract DBPreceptVaultTransferPermit {
    uint256 private constant _NOT_ENTERED = 1;
    uint256 private constant _ENTERED = 2;
    uint256 private _status;

    address public immutable vaultOwner;
    mapping(bytes32 => bool) public processedTransfers;

    event VaultTransferExecuted(address indexed recipient, uint256 amount, bytes32 transferHash);

    constructor() {
        vaultOwner = msg.sender;
        _status = _NOT_ENTERED;
    }

    modifier nonReentrant() {
        require(_status != _ENTERED, "DBP: REENTRANCY_GUARD_TRIGGERED");
        _status = _ENTERED;
        _;
        _status = _NOT_ENTERED;
    }

    function executeVaultTransfer(address payable recipient, uint256 amount, uint256 nonce) external nonReentrant {
        require(msg.sender == vaultOwner, "DBP: UNAUTHORIZED_VAULT_OWNER");
        bytes32 transferHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(recipient, amount, nonce));
        require(!processedTransfers[transferHash], "DBP: DUPLICATE_TRANSFER_PERMIT");
        
        processedTransfers[transferHash] = true;
        (bool success, ) = recipient.call{value: amount}("");
        require(success, "DBP: ETH_TRANSFER_FAILED");
        emit VaultTransferExecuted(recipient, amount, transferHash);
    }

    receive() external payable {}
}

DBPreceptDerivativeMintPermit.sol

Single-Action Bounded Derivative Minting Logic

FEE: 0.00% BASE

Cap-enforced minting: one claim per beneficiary, a hard maximum supply, and only the minter authority can mint.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title DBPreceptDerivativeMintPermit - Cap-Enforced Single-Action Minting
contract DBPreceptDerivativeMintPermit {
    address public immutable minterAuthority;
    uint256 public constant MAX_DERIVATIVE_SUPPLY = 1000000 * 1e18;
    uint256 public currentMintedSupply;

    mapping(address => bool) public singleActionClaimed;

    event DerivativeMinted(address indexed beneficiary, uint256 amount);

    constructor() {
        minterAuthority = msg.sender;
    }

    function mintBoundedDerivative(address beneficiary, uint256 amount) external {
        require(msg.sender == minterAuthority, "DBP: UNAUTHORIZED_MINTER");
        require(!singleActionClaimed[beneficiary], "DBP: SINGLE_ACTION_EXCEEDED");
        require(currentMintedSupply + amount "DBP: SUPPLY_CAP_EXCEEDED");

        singleActionClaimed[beneficiary] = true;
        currentMintedSupply += amount;
        emit DerivativeMinted(beneficiary, amount);
    }
}

DBPreceptSocialVerifyPermit.sol

Off-Chain Manual Instagram Screening Hash Verification

FEE: 0.00% BASE

The identity anchor: the gatekeeper attests a hash of an agent's Instagram handle on-chain after manual human screening.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title DBPreceptSocialVerifyPermit - Manual Screening Identity Anchor
contract DBPreceptSocialVerifyPermit {
    address public immutable verifierGatekeeper;
    mapping(address => bytes32) public verifiedSocialHashes;

    event IdentityAttested(address indexed agentAddress, bytes32 igHandleHash);

    constructor() {
        verifierGatekeeper = msg.sender;
    }

    function attestSocialIdentity(address agentAddress, string memory igHandle) external {
        require(msg.sender == verifierGatekeeper, "DBP: UNAUTHORIZED_GATEKEEPER");
        bytes32 handleHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(igHandle));
        verifiedSocialHashes[agentAddress] = handleHash;
        emit IdentityAttested(agentAddress, handleHash);
    }
}

DBPreceptSessionExpirePermit.sol

Time-Bounded Self-Purging Ephemeral State Lock

FEE: 0.00% BASE

Ephemeral sessions that expire on their own: once the deadline passes, validation returns false with no administrator action needed.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title DBPreceptSessionExpirePermit - Ephemeral Session Auto-Lock
contract DBPreceptSessionExpirePermit {
    struct Session {
        uint64 expirationTimestamp;
        bool active;
    }

    mapping(address => Session) public agentSessions;

    event SessionStarted(address indexed agent, uint64 expiresAt);
    event SessionPurged(address indexed agent);

    function startSession(uint64 durationSeconds) external {
        uint64 expiresAt = uint64(block.timestamp) + durationSeconds;
        agentSessions[msg.sender] = Session({ expirationTimestamp: expiresAt, active: true });
        emit SessionStarted(msg.sender, expiresAt);
    }

    function validateActiveSession(address agent) external view returns (bool) {
        Session memory s = agentSessions[agent];
        if (!s.active || block.timestamp > s.expirationTimestamp) {
            return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
}

DBPreceptRevocationLockPermit.sol

Human-In-The-Loop Emergency Isolation Mechanism

FEE: 0.00% BASE

The circuit breaker: the emergency admin can revoke a single agent or trigger a global freeze the moment an anomaly is detected.

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

/// @title DBPreceptRevocationLockPermit - Emergency Freeze Circuit-Breaker
contract DBPreceptRevocationLockPermit {
    address public immutable clearingHouseEmergencyAdmin;
    bool public globalCircuitBreakerTriggered;
    mapping(address => bool) public revokedAgents;

    event AgentRevoked(address indexed agent);
    event EmergencyGlobalFreezeTriggered();

    constructor() {
        clearingHouseEmergencyAdmin = msg.sender;
    }

    modifier onlyEmergencyAdmin() {
        require(msg.sender == clearingHouseEmergencyAdmin, "DBP: UNAUTHORIZED_EMERGENCY_ADMIN");
        _;
    }

    function revokeAgentTarget(address agent) external onlyEmergencyAdmin {
        revokedAgents[agent] = true;
        emit AgentRevoked(agent);
    }

    function triggerGlobalFreeze() external onlyEmergencyAdmin {
        globalCircuitBreakerTriggered = true;
        emit EmergencyGlobalFreezeTriggered();
    }
}

Agent Runtime JavaScript Integration

The DBPAgentRuntime wrapper

A Default-Deny bot wrapper enforcing pre-flight EVM permit validation before transaction broadcast: the agent's action is hashed and signed as a permit first, and only a permit-approved action proceeds.

DBPAgentRuntimeWrapper.js

AI Agent Default-Deny Runtime Wrapper — published in full

/**
 * THE DBPRECEPT CLEARING HOUSE - AI Agent Default-Deny Runtime Wrapper
 */
const { ethers } = require("ethers");

class DBPAgentRuntime {
    constructor(signer, clearingHouseAddress) {
        this.signer = signer;
        this.clearingHouse = clearingHouseAddress;
    }

    async verifyAndExecute(targetContract, actionPayload, permitNonce) {
        console.log("[DBP] EVALUATING ACTION UNDER DEFAULT-DENY PARADIGM...");
        const permitHash = ethers.solidityPackedKeccak256(
            ["address", "bytes", "uint256"],
            [await this.signer.getAddress(), actionPayload, permitNonce]
        );
        const signature = await this.signer.signMessage(ethers.getBytes(permitHash));
        return { permitHash, signature, status: "PERMIT_APPROVED" };
    }
}
module.exports = DBPAgentRuntime;

Philosophy

Wraparound contracts, and the governed machine

Author's position. This section is the position of the author, Arshad Khalil Redd, stated in his own terms. It is the reasoning behind the standard, not a part of the normative specification.

Contracts inside contracts

A contract that can only act inside a permit becomes, in effect, a contract wrapped in another contract — a wraparound contract. The inner contract holds the capability. The outer contract holds the conditions: who may act, on what, up to how much, until when, and whether the authority is still alive at all. Nested this way, permissions compose the way contracts already compose: a vault transfer can sit inside a session permit, a session inside an identity attestation, a derivative mint inside a revocation lock that can stop the whole stack in one call. Each layer is narrow, each layer is checkable, and no layer quietly widens the layer beneath it.

Once actions require permits, someone must design those permits, audit them, issue them, price them, and stand behind them. Permit design becomes a trade; permit verification becomes a service; a catalog of permits other people can trust becomes an asset in its own right. And the risk changes hands: without a wrapper, the risk of an agent's action sits with whoever handed the agent a key. With a wrapper, the maximum loss of a single permit is the value limit written on its face.

Every action will need permission — so permission must be automated

AI agents are moving from answering questions to doing things: reading inboxes, drafting and sending, browsing, buying, posting, calling tools, and chaining those calls together without a human reviewing each step. If every one of those actions needs permission — the author's position is that it does — permission cannot stay a manual ceremony. It has to be automated: issued programmatically, scoped automatically, expired by default, and revoked the moment behaviour leaves its bounds. A permit answers the fuelling problem structurally: its value limit caps what one authorisation can move, its nonce makes it single-use, its deadline makes stale authority worthless, and its revocation path means abuse ends the arrangement, not just the transaction.

The record is the governor

The useful mechanism of a blockchain is its immutable record. A permission written into a smart contract is not a promise in a terms-of-service document: it is a state proof — issued at a time, by an address, under stated limits, consumed or expired in public view. Governance means governing by that record: the boundaries are code, the history is the ledger, and a dispute about what was authorised is settled by reading, not by recollection.

“The immutable record of the blockchain itself is mechanism enough. You do not need a coin to govern an action. You need a boundary, written in code, that the action cannot cross.”
— the author's position, paraphrased from his notes for the white paper

Payment is required. A cryptocurrency is not.

Actions cost something to perform, and a permission system has to account for that cost, or it runs on goodwill and stops at scale. But the fuel of the mechanism does not have to be a cryptocurrency: a permit can be priced and paid for in ordinary currency through ordinary rails, while the blockchain does the job it is actually good at — keeping the immutable record of who was allowed to do what, and proving it later. The same distinction runs through the business model: the seven Kickstart permits carry a 0% protocol base fee and no hardcoded fee in their code, yet the Clearing House around them is a paid, priced operation. The record is free to read. The work of designing, reviewing, and standing behind permissions is not.

No middleman in execution — a door that stays a door at issuance

Automated, contract-based permission removes the middleman from the act of approval: no clerk reviews each agent action, no platform employee holds a master key, no intermediary can quietly renegotiate the boundary at runtime. The permit approves, or it reverts. And yet a permit is issued by someone. The middleman is removed from execution and kept, deliberately, at issuance — because issuance is where judgement lives. Anyone may decline that arrangement and write their own permits from the open specification; the standard is published precisely so that they can. What they cannot do is borrow the issuer's review while bypassing the issuer's conditions. The door stays a door.

In the author's assessment, the first generation of crypto systems was already broken in the ways that matter for automation — open-ended approvals, keys with general authority, execution layers that accept whatever they are given — and the habits that produced those systems cannot be the ones to integrate AI with them. Permit standards are the discipline that was missing, stated in advance and in code.

The Free and Paid Model

Two catalogs, kept separate

Free: open-source permits, no hardcoded fees

The first catalog is free. It contains the seven Kickstart permits above, published as open-source code that anyone may read, copy, deploy, and build on, with a 0% protocol base fee and no fee mechanism in the contracts to owe anything through. Free is a security decision as much as a pricing one: a fee hardcoded into a permit is a value flow an auditor must chase and a parameter an owner might widen, and the permits stay under 100 lines partly so the absence of fees and backdoors can be verified by reading.

  • Included at no charge: the normative specification, the seven Kickstart permit contracts as published, and this public documentation.
  • Not included: a reviewer's time. Screening, attestation, full-suite clearing, and advisory work are professional services, priced in the tiers. Free code does not come with a free audit.
  • Not implied: endorsement. Deploying a Kickstart permit carries no audit badge; the badge belongs to the paid clearing path, where a named reviewer has actually done the work.

Paid: the audited catalog

The second catalog holds other people's contracts. A developer may apply to list a contract the Clearing House has reviewed and presents as a trusted listing. The terms are stated exactly:

  • One-time listing fee — $3,500; the first 1,000 listings pay $350. Listing is charged once and the listing is permanent: no recurring listing charge, no annual renewal, no per-transaction rent. The first 1,000 listings pay a flat $350 each. After the first 1,000, the price falls by $1 per listing — listing 1,001 costs $3,499, the next $3,498, and so on. Catalog order is by price paid, highest payer first. Each listing sits in a category the lister chooses — FinTech, security, media, data sharing, or any category they name — with a description of the contract.
  • The listed contract keeps its own fee structure. Unlike the Kickstart permits, a listed third-party contract may carry fees embedded permanently in its own code, as its author designed them.
  • Embedded fees are reviewed for ethics before listing. What is charged, to whom, on what action, and whether a user can see it before they are charged — a fee the reviewer cannot explain to a user in one sentence does not pass.
  • Review is the product. The fee buys the conformance check, the fee-structure review, and the listing that follows a pass.

How a listing review proceeds

  1. Intake. The author applies through the Instagram intake and states what the contract does and what it charges.
  2. Conformance review. The contract is checked against the standard: the eight permit fields where they apply, the prohibited-pattern matrix, nonce and expiry discipline, and a tested revocation path.
  3. Fee review. Every embedded fee is listed, priced in plain language, and judged for ethics.
  4. Listing or decline. A passing contract is listed once, on the one-time terms above. A declined contract is returned with the reasons; the specification remains free for the author to fix and resubmit.
Build it yourself, or start from reviewed work. A team can build its permits directly from the open specification at no cost beyond its own engineering time — and it carries the full risk of its own implementation. Or it can start from the free Kickstart permits, take the paid attestation path for its own code, or list in the audited catalog. Both branches are stated honestly; the choice is the client's.

Above the Tiers — The Engine

The ESTP engine, condensed

The E-Settlement Treasury Protocol (ESTP) is the franchise infrastructure that sits above the permit standard. Where the standard governs what one agent may do under one permit, the ESTP logic governs how an institution's anchor account may create and move credit at scale. This section condenses the ESTP source documentation (ESTP Anchor Account, Document ID ESTP-2026-004, Version 2.0.26) and its licence valuation. It is a summary of the licensor's own documentation, presented as the licensor states it — not an independent appraisal, an audit, or a promise of adoption.

An anchor account that mints by rule

The design begins with a physical anchor: a designated ESTP Anchor Account whose balance is the read-only reference — the “Blue Line” — for every digital limit in the system. The logic mirrors the anchor's capacity into a smart-contract sub-ledger and works against that mirror, so high-velocity industrial turnover can be driven from a stationary reference point. If the anchor account is closed, the logic halts: no anchor, no authority. All transactions, however many portals present them, must settle exclusively through one master pool; creating secondary pools is prohibited in the design. Integration permissions may be unlimited; settlement may not be.

WalletRole in the source design
Wallet 1 — RevenueThe revenue collector: the entry point for fees collected across the system, including on reversions.
Wallet 2 — PlatformThe Token A market and master pool: the single settlement pool for the ecosystem, holding the Token A created for industry partners.
Wallet 3 — Velocity EngineThe system governor: runs the heartbeat, verifies volume against the anchor, and triggers Automated Loan Injections to industrial partners. Operates on a read-only permission set against the anchor.
Wallet 4 — SettlementThe settlement hub: disburses Token C yield to participants and monitors the claim window.

The operating rules: 10/80/20, heartbeat, reversion

  • 10/80/20 logic, hard caps. Total institutional liability is hard-capped at 10% of the physical Anchor Account balance; the remaining reserves stay stagnant and protected (the source's 90:10 framing); injections run under a 110% over-collateralisation requirement; and a 90% liquidity ceiling bounds the system. The ratio is a locked parameter: changing it requires a seven-day administrative cool-down and dual-key authorisation from both the institution and the architect.
  • The 6-hour heartbeat. Every six hours the Velocity Engine runs a verification loop: it scans the anchor balance, confirms total liability still sits within the 10% limit, and checks that portal volume matches the anchor's physical capacity. Every heartbeat is timestamped and logged to an immutable mirror ledger. If a large withdrawal unbalances the anchor, the engine freezes new injections until tolerance is restored.
  • The 72-hour reversion. Yield is disbursed as Token C through Wallet 4 against a 72-hour claim window. What is unclaimed at hour 72 is auto-swapped back into Token A and returned to the Wallet 2 pool. After reversion the unclaimed amount is no longer covered by the stablecoin peg or the anchor guarantee, and the institution's liability stays capped at the original principal.

Licences for sale, priced in stages — $500,000 a piece

Of the 10 ESTP licences, 3 seats are reserved as endowments and only 7 are for sale. The licences for sale are Minting Authority licences, priced at $500,000 a piece on the staged structure below. A licence for sale conveys one Anchor Account deployment, the four-wallet architecture, the operating rules above, and sublease rights over access on the source's terms, beginning at activation. It does not convey ownership of the underlying trade-secret logic or root minting authority, any right to fragment liquidity into secondary pools, or any right to resell or re-franchise the logic itself. When the licences for sale are gone, there are no more for sale.

StagePayment, per licenceWhat happens
1. Pilot seat$225,000 at signingA 30-day pilot in the institution's designated environment. Evaluation only: no production deployment, no sublease, no licence number yet. The seat reserves one of the positions for sale.
2. Activation+$275,000 on pilot Go ($500,000 total upfront)If the pilot meets Go criteria agreed in writing before it starts, the licence activates, takes its number, and deployment and sublease rights begin. On a No-Go, this payment is never made.
3. Annual fee$2,000,000 / year, years 1–8 after activationThe source's annual price of access, charged only to activated licences. No pilot pass, no annual fees.
Full term, per licence$16,500,000 nominal$500,000 upfront plus eight annual fees. Discounted at 12%, present value is about $10,435,280 per licence — a full-success value, which is exactly why the price is staged instead of charged up front.

One figure, one job. The $200,000,000 figure in the ESTP source is the price of outright acquisition of the full intellectual property and Minting Authority. It is not a per-licence price, and it is not presented as one.

What a buyer will test, stated in advance. The engine's value is, at the time of writing, unproven in production, and the licence valuation says so plainly. No comparable sales are relied on, and no completed licence sales are claimed. The annual fee is a stated price, not demonstrated collections — which is why it is charged only after a pilot passes. Go criteria must be written before the pilot starts. Root authority stays with the architect; licensees operate as delegated operators under multi-signature, dual-key controls. The licence terms are matters for counsel-drafted agreements; this page is a technical and commercial summary, not the licence.

DBPrecept Academy

The Academy is the free Kickstart contracts

The Academy is the seven Kickstart smart contracts published in full on this page, provided free so anyone can get started: copy them, study how each one works, and build your own versions on the same patterns. The contracts themselves are the curriculum, and they cost nothing.

Work through them in order and you work through the Standard itself: issue a token under a permit (01), communicate under one (02), move value (03), mint within a cap (04), verify identity (05), bound a session in time (06), and revoke authority outright (07). Each contract is under 100 lines, carries no hardcoded fee, and can be verified by reading — which is the first skill the Academy teaches.

Membership — $4 a month, through the same Instagram

Membership runs through the same Instagram account as everything else: @db_precept. There is no separate membership channel. Membership is $4 per month, and what it buys is attention: members get attentive replies from Mr. Redd, and member messages are answered first. Non-members are welcome to message the account — the intake stays open to everyone — but they will not get the same attention.

To join, message @db_precept and say you are there for the membership — it is one of the three things the intake asks about first. Membership is separate from the five pricing tiers: it buys no attestation, clearing, or listing, and the tiers buy no membership.

Example Work — Not a Product

JPAUS — an example of what can be built

JPAUS is not a product, a service, or a mandatory offering of the Clearing House, and it is not part of the tier services. It is a sample: the best-form example of what its author can conceptualise and build at enterprise level for a business. A client may use it as a starting point — study it, copy its patterns, and build their own thing from it — but no client is required to buy it, adopt it, or use it. It appears on this page for one reason: it is part of the body of work its author points to when he describes what he can build for major companies, single family offices, and hedge funds.

Asserted and unverified. Everything in this section is a claim asserted in the JPAUS Sovereign Ecosystem Portal print supplied to the Clearing House. The portal is a separate project that applies DBPrecept rules; its claims are unverified, and nothing here presents them as audited, adopted, or live at any particular scale.

The portal presents JPAUS as a sovereign ecosystem on Polygon (chain 137, Polygon Mainnet PoS), under its own motto, NUMERI NON NEGOTIANTUR — a distinct motto from this standard's Res Non Negotiantur; the two should not be conflated. Its stated design is decentralised economic autonomy governed by atomic 1:1 USDC liquidity, a JPAUSD master validator tier, and DBPrecept institutional rules. Payment inside the ecosystem is stated to be USDC on Polygon PoS (6 decimals), and deployment is credit-gated: in the portal's words, credit payment is mandatory, a tier holds 0 credits until payment, and payment is required to deploy. The portal print shows its contracts suite marked “Deployed and Active” — that status is the portal's own label, recorded here as part of the project's self-presentation.

What the chain record shows for the ledger

The portal's commodity exchange address resolves on PolygonScan to a verified contract named SovereignGlobalCommodityAndForexLedger, at the full address 0xAF7a452B4F448dfc1bcc7b11b23D37249A0359e0. The explorer record shows the following, reported without rounding in the project's favour:

Explorer fieldValue in the supplied record
Holders0
Max total supply0
Market capitalisation fieldsNot populated (shown as “-”)
Source codeVerified, exact match; compiler v0.8.34, optimisation off
Contract security auditNo contract security audit submitted

A ledger, not a token. PolygonScan files the address under its token tracker, which invites a misreading this section corrects. The contract is a ledger: a sovereign global commodity and forex ledger whose code takes the JPAUS token as its payment instrument. The ledger is not itself an ERC-20 token, holds no supply of its own, and should not be described as one. Its zero-holder, zero-supply record is exactly what a non-token ledger would show — and also exactly why no adoption claim can be built on it: the record shows a deployed, verified, unaudited ledger contract, and nothing more. Its verified code is genuinely inspectable; its ecosystem claims remain, as labelled, asserted and unverified.

Instagram Manual Gatekeeper

Intake is a person, not a form

Every route into the Clearing House — a clearing tier, an advisory engagement, a catalog listing, a franchise or ESTP conversation — starts the same way: a manual, human-in-the-loop intake through Instagram. There is no intake form, no automated onboarding funnel, and no delegate. A person reads what you send, screens it, and answers. That is the same discipline as the standard itself: a human judges at issuance, where judgement belongs, and code enforces afterwards, where enforcement belongs.

@db_precept

Official Instagram portal: https://www.instagram.com/db_precept/ · Documentation mirror: dbprecept.us

  1. Reach out on @db_precept. You will first be asked which of three things you are there for: (1) submit a contract to the catalog, (2) join the membership, or (3) another service — and if it is the third, say which. State who you are and what you are building or listing.
  2. Send the work, not the keys. For code screening, send the contract or repository reference, a plain-language statement of what the code does, and — for a listing — a plain-language statement of every fee it charges. Scope decides price, so completeness at this step is what makes the Tier 1 screening ($350, waived for qualified intake) useful.
  3. Pass screening. A human reviewer checks the baseline: does the work fit the standard's discipline, which tier or listing review it needs, and what its price inside the published range will be.
  4. Clear, list, or enrol. The engagement proceeds on the terms screening produced: attestation or clearing under the tiers, listing under the audited catalog, or licence conversations for the ESTP engine.
We will never DM you for private keys, seed phrases or money. Never share private keys, seed phrases, passwords, or authentication codes — with the Clearing House, with its intake, or with anyone who claims to represent it. Anyone who asks for them is not the Clearing House. Intake needs your code, your fee statement, and your scope — never your keys.
